region: Mountains of Lebanon, Syria and Turkey; planted in parks and estates in Europe
description: Cedar of Lebanon is a true cedar with fragrant, light brown, fairly soft wood. In the UK it is mostly available from felled park and estate trees and is used for joinery, garden furniture, gates and turning.

hazards.summary: The UK HSE lists cedar of Lebanon as a cause of breathing problems and rhinitis. A 1972 case report described respiratory symptoms after only brief exposure to its dust; a later review classes this as a non-allergic (not IgE-driven) reaction.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses. This applies to this wood like every other species.

related_species_note: Not related to western red cedar or eastern white cedar (Thuja), which have their own entries and different evidence.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed cedar of Lebanon (Cedrus libani) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Light brown to warm yellowish-brown heartwood with a slightly darker reddish tone in places, and paler cream sapwood along one edge. Distinct growth rings with a fairly sharp earlywood-to-latewood contrast, medium texture, occasional small tight knots, a soft satin luster, and no visible pores. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.

notes_internal: Greenberg-1972 has no abstract on PubMed; claim relies on its title and the Schlunssen-2018 Table 1 classification (RS, not sIgE-mediated). Paper itself not read. Greenberg's title uses the misspelling 'Cedra libani'. Level 2 comes from HSE-WIS30.
